items.title: PPU
items.text: GBA PPU notes from Sly. GBATEK is the actual reference, this is the stuff I needed to know plus gotchas

items.title: Timing
items.text:
• 1'232 cycles per line, 228 lines per frame (160 visible + 68 VBLANK) = 280'896 cycles, ~59.73 FPS
  • 240 visible pixels at 4 cycles each, but the HBLANK flag/IRQ only happens around cycle 1'006-1'008 (not 960!)
  • VCOUNT (0x04000006) current line, DISPSTAT (0x04000004) IRQs for HBLANK, VBLANK, VCOUNT match

Games change registers between lines (HBLANK IRQ or HBLANK DMA) for per-line scroll, windows, affine matrices etc. Rendering a whole frame with the final register values loses all of that. I render each visible line at HBLANK with the state at that point. Mid-line changes would need finer timing.

items.title: DISPCNT
items.text:
0-2     Mode
3       CGB mode (BIOS only)
4       Displayed page (bitmap modes)
5       OAM access during HBLANK
6       Sprite tile mapping (0=2D, 1=1D)
7       Forced blank
8-12    BG0-BG3, OBJ enable
13-15   WIN0, WIN1, OBJ window enable

mode    BG0     BG1     BG2         BG3
-----------------------------------------------
0       text    text    text        text
1       text    text    affine      -
2       -       -       affine      affine
3       -       -       240x160 16bpp, 1 page
4       -       -       240x160 8bpp (palette), 2 pages
5       -       -       160x128 16bpp, 2 pages

Bitmap modes always draw on BG2 (bit 10 must be set) and use BG2's affine parameters, so bitmaps can be rotated/scaled too.

items.title: Bitmap Modes
items.text:
• Mode 3/5: pixel is the 15-bit color directly
  • Mode 4: pixel is a palette index, 0x06000000 + 240y + x (page 1 at +0xA000)
  • Mode 4 index 0 is transparent (backdrop/sprites behind BG2 show through), same for area around a mode 5 image
  • Bitmap modes eat the first half of OBJ VRAM, sprite tiles are limited to 512-1023
  • Outside of a bitmap is always transparent, wraparound bit is ignored

items.title: 8-bit VRAM Writes
items.text:
VRAM can't be written 8 bits at a time. An strb to the BG area is duplicated into both bytes of the halfword, an strb to the OBJ area is ignored. Source

fn write_vram(&mut self, mut address: u32, width: Width, value: u32) {
    if width == Width::Byte {
        if self::vram_offset(address) >= self.obj_offset() {
            return;
        }

        address &= !1;
        self::write_memory(&mut self.vram, address + 1, width, value, self::vram_offset);
    }

    self::write_memory(&mut self.vram, address, width, value, self::vram_offset);
}

Note: OBJ area boundary depends on mode (0x10000 in tiled modes, 0x14000 in bitmap modes).

items.title: Colors
items.text:
0-4     Red
5-9     Green
10-14   Blue
15      unused

BG palette at 0x05000000, OBJ palette at 0x05000200. Entry 0 of the BG palette is the backdrop.

5 to 8 bit: (c << 3) | (c >> 2), otherwise 31 becomes 248 instead of 255.

items.title: Text Backgrounds
items.text:
BGxCNT
0-1     Priority
2-3     Tile block (16 KiB)
6       Mosaic
7       8bpp
8-12    Map block (2 KiB)
13      Wraparound (affine only)
14-15   Map size
  • 4bpp: 32-byte tiles, low nibble is the left pixel, 16 banks of 16 colors
  • 8bpp: 64-byte tiles, full 256-color palette
  • Index 0 is transparent in every bank
map entry
0-9     Tile number
10      H flip
11      V flip
12-15   Palette bank

Maps are stored in 32x32 entry blocks (2 KiB), not as one big row-major array!

size    pixels      blocks
-------------------------------------------
0       256x256     SC0
1       512x256     SC0 SC1
2       256x512     SC0 / SC1
3       512x512     SC0 SC1 / SC2 SC3

block  = (ty / 32) * (W / 256) + (tx / 32)
offset = 2 * (32 * (ty % 32) + tx % 32)
entry  = 0x06000000 + 2048 * (map_block + block) + offset

Scroll (BGxHOFS/BGxVOFS, 9 bits) wraps at the map size, e.g. HOFS 337 on a 256 wide map is 81:

let bg_x = (x + bg.hofs as usize) & (width - 1);

Flipped tiles use 7 - px / 7 - py. Palette entry is 16 * bank + index for 4bpp.

items.title: Sprites (OBJ)
items.text:
OAM at 0x07000000, 128 entries of 8 bytes, 4th halfword belongs to affine matrices.

attr0
0-7     Y
8       Affine
9       Hide (regular) / double size (affine)
10-11   Mode (normal, semi-transparent, OBJ window)
12      Mosaic
13      8bpp
14-15   Shape (square, wide, tall, -)

attr1
0-8     X
9-13    Affine matrix number (affine)
12      H flip (regular)
13      V flip (regular)
14-15   Size

attr2
0-9     Tile number
10-11   Priority
12-15   Palette bank

size    square    wide     tall
------------------------------------
0       8x8       16x8     8x16
1       16x16     32x8     8x32
2       32x32     32x16    16x32
3       64x64     64x32    32x64
  • OBJ tiles at 0x06010000 + 32n. Tile numbers count 32-byte units even for 8bpp, so 8bpp sprites should use even numbers (lowest bit ignored in 2D mapping)
  • 1D mapping: n + ty * (w / 8) + tx
  • 2D mapping: n + 32 * ty + tx
  • 8bpp: column offset doubles in both, row offset doubles in 1D only

items.title: Position Wrap
items.text:
Y is 8 bits and wraps, X is 9 bits and wraps at 512. A sprite at y = 247 with height 32 shows up at the top of the screen.

let row = (line as u8).wrapping_sub(attr.y_coordinate()) as usize;
if row >= height {
    continue;
}

Affine double size sprites have a Y wrapping exception.

items.title: Sprite vs Sprite
items.text:
Lower priority number wins, on tie the lower OAM index wins. Iterating from entry 0 up, a later opaque pixel only replaces one with a higher priority number. mGBA issue

if dst.is_none_or(|pixel| attr.priority() < pixel.priority) {

items.title: Cycle Budget
items.text: 1'210 cycles per line, 954 if DISPCNT bit 5 is set. Regular sprite costs 1 cycle per pixel of width, affine costs 10 + 2 * area width. Once the budget runs out the rest of the line has no sprites, and offscreen sprites still count. Source

items.title: Layer Priority
items.text:
• Lower priority number in front, on tie lower BG number wins
  • Sprite goes in front of BGs with the same or higher priority number
  • Backdrop is behind everything (treat it as priority u8::MAX)
bg_order.sort_by_key(|&(_, priority)| priority); // stable sort keeps BG order on ties

let (mut color, bg_priority) = bg_order
    .iter()
    .find_map(|&(index, priority)| bg_lines[index][x].map(|color| (color, priority)))
    .unwrap_or((backdrop, u8::MAX));

if let Some(sprite) = sprite_line[x]
    && sprite.priority <= bg_priority
{
    color = sprite.color;
}

Blending also needs the layer right behind the top one, so track the top 2.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
WINxH   0-7 X2 (right + 1)    8-15 X1 (left)
WINxV   0-7 Y2 (bottom + 1)   8-15 Y1 (top)

WININ   0-5 WIN0 (BG0-3, OBJ, effects)    8-13 WIN1
WINOUT  0-5 outside                       8-13 OBJ window
  • Check order: WIN0 -> WIN1 -> OBJ window -> outside. First match wins
  • OBJ window = opaque pixels of sprites with mode OBJ window (not drawn themselves). Needs DISPCNT bit 12 and 15
  • No window enabled at all -> everything visible, effects allowed everywhere
  • A layer still has to be enabled in DISPCNT
if let Some(index) = (0..2).find(|&index| windows.contains(index, x, y)) {
    return Some(WindowRegion::Rectangle(index));
}

Some(if windows.obj_enabled && inside_obj_window {
    WindowRegion::Obj
} else {
    WindowRegion::Outside
})

items.title: Blending
items.text:
BLDCNT
0-5     1st target (BG0-3, OBJ, BD)
6-7     Effect (0=none, 1=alpha, 2=brighten, 3=darken)
8-13    2nd target (BG0-3, OBJ, BD)

Only the topmost and the layer right behind it matter. Alpha needs top = 1st target and below = 2nd target.

alpha:     I = min(31, (I1 * EVA + I2 * EVB) >> 4)
brighten:  I = I + (((31 - I) * EVY) >> 4)
darken:    I = I - ((I * EVY) >> 4)
  • EVA/EVB (BLDALPHA bits 0-4 / 8-12) and EVY (BLDY) treat 17-31 as 16
  • EVA + EVB can exceed 16, hence the min(31)
  • Semi-transparent sprites alpha blend with the layer behind if it's a 2nd target, regardless of BLDCNT's 1st targets and effect
  • Sprites can't blend with each other (already reduced to one sprite pixel)
  • Window effects bit must be set in the pixel's region

items.title: Mosaic
items.text:
MOSAIC
0-3     BG width - 1
4-7     BG height - 1
8-11    OBJ width - 1
12-15   OBJ height - 1

Enabled per BG (BGxCNT bit 6) and per sprite (attr0 bit 12). BG blocks are aligned to the screen and take the top-left pixel's color, i.e. round the screen position down to the block start before lookup.

items.title: Affine Backgrounds
items.text:
Differences to text BGs:

  • Always 8bpp, BGxCNT bit 7 ignored
  • Map entry is 1 byte (tile number only, no flips/banks), max 256 tiles
  • Map is square and plain row-major, no 32x32 blocks
  • Scroll registers are ignored
size    pixels        map bytes
---------------------------------
0       128x128       256
1       256x256       1'024
2       512x512       4'096
3       1024x1024     16'384

The PPU walks from the screen back into the background. Parameters are signed 8.8 fixed point (BGxPA-PD, write only), reference point BGxX/BGxY is signed 20.8 (28 bits):

px = X + PA*x + PB*y
py = Y + PC*x + PD*y
texel = (px >> 8, py >> 8)

Bigger parameter = smaller picture (it's texels per pixel, not a zoom factor). For clockwise rotation θ with magnification s:

PA =  256*cos(θ)/s     PB = 256*sin(θ)/s
PC = -256*sin(θ)/s     PD = 256*cos(θ)/s

Note: GBATEK gives PB and PC the same sign, for a normal rotation they should be negatives of each other.

To keep BG point (cx, cy) at screen point (sx, sy):

X = 256*cx - PA*sx - PB*sy
Y = 256*cy - PC*sx - PD*sy

Wraparound (BGxCNT bit 13) off -> outside of the map is transparent. Masking with all ones when off lets negative coordinates become huge usize and get caught by the same bounds check:

for dst in output.iter_mut() {
    let tx = ((x >> 8) as usize) & wrap_mask;
    let ty = ((y >> 8) as usize) & wrap_mask;
    x += matrix.pa;
    y += matrix.pc;

    if tx >= size || ty >= size {
        continue;
    }
    // ...
}

items.title: Internal Reference Points
items.text:
The above reference points are automatically copied to internal registers during each [VBLANK], specifying the origin for the first scanline. The internal registers are then incremented by dmx and dmy after each scanline. Source

  • Copy BGxX/BGxY to internal registers at VBLANK
  • Add PB/PD to the internal ones after every line
  • Writing BGxX/BGxY mid-frame updates the internal register immediately
/// Advances the internal reference points by PB/PD to the start of the next scanline.
fn step_reference_points(&mut self) {
    for i in 0..2 {
        let [_, pb, _, pd] = self.bg_matrix[i];
        self.bg_ref_internal[i][0] += pb.value();
        self.bg_ref_internal[i][1] += pd.value();
    }
}

fn reload_reference_points(&mut self) {
    self.bg_ref_internal = self.bg_ref.map(|point| point.map(ReferencePoint::value));
}

Using Y + PD*line instead of the internal register breaks anything that writes the matrix or reference point per line (mode 7 style roads).

items.title: Affine Sprites
items.text:
• Bit 9 of attr0 means double size, affine sprites can't be hidden with it
  • No flip bits, negate PA+PB (H) or PC+PD (V) instead
  • 32 matrices in OAM, matrix m: PA at 0x07000006 + 32m, PB/PC/PD each 8 bytes after
  • Transform is around the center of the sprite and the center of its on-screen area
  • Double size makes the area 2w x 2h, position is top left of that, center at (x + w, y + h)
tx = ((PA*dx + PB*dy) >> 8) + w/2
ty = ((PC*dx + PD*dy) >> 8) + h/2

dx/dy measured from the area center. Texels outside the sprite are transparent.

let (x, y) = if let Some(matrix) = matrix {
    let dx = col as i32 - (box_width / 2) as i32;
    let (tx, ty) = matrix.apply(dx, dy);
    let x = tx + (width / 2) as i32;
    let y = ty + (height / 2) as i32;

    let (Ok(x), Ok(y)) = (usize::try_from(x), usize::try_from(y)) else {
        continue;
    };

    if x >= width || y >= height {
        continue;
    }

    (x, y)
} else {
    attr.flip(col, row)
};

items.title: Test Scenes
items.text:
Games that exercise one specific feature really well:

  • OpenLara: mode 4 page flipping (DISPCNT alternating 0x0404/0x0414)
  • Game Boy Advance Video cartridges: mode 3, 1000+ colors in a frame
  • Shaman King: Master of Spirits: 4 text BGs with priorities, scrolling clouds
  • Action Man: Robot Atak: mode 3 + sprites (tiles >= 512) on the map, 1D mapping, Y-wrapped health bar sprite
  • Tales of Phantasia intro: WIN0/WIN1 reveal, darken fade restricted to WIN1 via effects bit
  • Fire Emblem title: OBJ window (WINOUT = 0x313e), per-line BG0 scroll, alpha blend on lines 40-99
  • Golden Sun opening: alpha blending with EVA + EVB > 16 (BLDALPHA = 0x1006)
  • The Minish Cap intro: alpha fade with window effect bit masking the picture
  • Super Mario World level entry: BG mosaic 0x1111 to 0xFFFF, sprites unaffected
  • Wario Land 4: Nintendo logo (affine scale), vortex (affine BG + double size affine sprite)
  • F-Zero: Maximum Velocity: mode switch at line 32, HBLANK DMA writing BG2 matrix + reference point every line

Writeups: Part 1: Bitmaps, Tiles and Palettes, Part 2: Layers, Sprites and Blending, Part 3: Rotation, Scaling and Perspective

items.title: GX
items.text: GX (Flipper/Hollywood GPU) notes from Gecko, see Games for the bugs these caused

items.title: Vertex Skip
items.text:
An indexed position with all bits set means "skip this vertex":

format    reserved index    meaning
----------------------------------------
8-bit     0xFF              skip vertex
16-bit    0xFFFF            skip vertex

Only applies to the indexed position field! Other fields use 0xFF according to their own format (e.g. alpha 0xFF = opaque). Documented in Nintendo's US6700586B1 patent.

A skipped record doesn't occupy a corner in the strip, so 0, 1, SKIP, 2, 3 is the same quad as 0, 1, 2, 3.

The bytes still exist though! E.g. 8-bit position index + RGBA color is 5 bytes, skipped or not. The parser must consume the full record (using the current vertex format), otherwise it reads a color byte as the next position index and loses its place:

for each vertex record in the draw:
    record = consume the complete record using the current format

    if its indexed position is the reserved all ones value:
        continue

    decode the record and append its vertex

assemble the draw's triangles from the retained vertices
  • Filter skipped records before vertex decoding
  • Update the vertex count per draw, otherwise a removed record can join one draw's vertices to the next
  • Depth plane tracking for z-freeze needs to agree on which triangles exist, so it has to run on the filtered list

Code: filter_skipped_vertices

Test: vertex-skip (direct, 8-bit and 16-bit indices, all 3 should match)

items.title: z-freeze
items.text:
Lets a draw reuse the depth plane of an earlier triangle instead of its own depth. libogc: GX_SetCoPlanar(GX_ENABLE).

  • While z-freeze is off, every triangle replaces the saved plane
  • While it's on, the last plane is kept and following draws evaluate it for depth (own outline/colors/UVs, borrowed depth)
  • The reference triangle doesn't need to write color or depth to establish a plane

Plane from the 3 screen space vertices:

depth(x, y) = A*x + B*y + C

Evaluated for every pixel of the new draw, including pixels outside the original triangle, so the result can leave the 0-1 range (see below). Degenerate (line/point) triangles don't define a plane.

Dolphin's January 2015 progress report also covers this.

items.title: Plane Overflow
items.text:
Clamping the extrapolated depth to max is wrong. Hardware readbacks (GX_ALWAYS write, GX_PeekZ read), horizontal and vertical slopes give the same values:

plane depth    Wii Z24     ~
----------------------------------
0.25           0x400000    0.25
1.25           0xFFFFFF    1
4.25           0x000000    0
8.25           0x3FF7E0    0.25
12.25          0x000000    0
16.25          0x3FEFC0    0.25

Looks like a value overflowing every 8 depth units before being clamped, which fits a signed 27-bit intermediate (2^27 / 2^24 = 8, range -4 to <+4):

  • 4.25 wraps to -3.75 -> clamped to 0
  • 8.25 is a full cycle -> back to 0.25

Note: wrapping with % 1.0 gives narrow stripes instead of the broad bands seen on hardware. 27-bit is just what matches, not proven, and some exact readings still differ.

Code: plane calculation, depth shader w/ overflow

Test: z-freeze (sloped planes), original 2-panel test

Honorary mention: hazelwiss (hardware testing)

items.title: TEV Wrapping
items.text:
TEV results must be reduced to 8 bits by wrapping (keep low byte), not clamping, and not left wide. Unclamped stages keep a signed intermediate of -1024..1023.

Where the wrap happens matters:

  • A/B/C inputs read only the low byte of a register
  • D input keeps the wide (signed) value
  • Final RGB/alpha output keeps the low byte before alpha test / blending

Making every stored register 8 bits loses information too early (breaks D).

  • Input wrapping alone fixes Sunshine but not Galaxy (the eye stage creates the overflow itself)
  • Output wrapping alone fixes Galaxy and makes Sunshine almost right (off by 2)

Other bits:

  • C factor is expanded to C + (C >> 7) before multiplying so 255 represents exactly 1
  • Scaled additions round by adding 128 before >> 8

Commit 14aae5a: integer arithmetic in the regular combiners, A/B/C inputs wrapped to 8 bits, final RGB/alpha wrapped before testing. Still a mixed implementation (combiner in ints, TEV registers as normalized floats), not sure yet what the implications are.

Dolphin: Pixel Processing Problems

items.title: Games
items.text: (mostly?) fixes for game issues in Gecko

items.title: Triangle Out of Luigi's Hand
items.text:
Thin triangle stretching from Luigi's hand across the character selection menu (look between Luigi's hand and Wario's portrait).

The affected triangle strip ended with a skip record (position index 0xFF). I fetched a position for it anyway and interpreted unrelated memory as:

[-27.166016, 15.875, 0.0]

Transforming that point and connecting it to the previous 2 corners produced the spike. A skipped record doesn't occupy a corner in the strip, so 0, 1, SKIP, 2, 3 should give the same quad as 0, 1, 2, 3.

Fix: remove skipped records before vertex decoding and update the vertex count for each draw, see Vertex Skip.

Writeup: vertex-skip: The Case of Luigi's Extra Triangle

items.title: Tops of Signs Missing
items.text:
Upper parts of the player selection signs (just below "MAIN MENU") are covered by the sky, with a straight cutoff. Geometry is all there, a later draw paints over it.

The menu does this:

  1. Draw a small shape to establish a depth plane
  2. Enable z-freeze
  3. Draw the sky over the top 112 framebuffer rows using that saved plane

Without z-freeze the sky uses its own near depth and covers the signs. That draw ends at row 112, hence the straight cutoff.

Saved plane:

Z24 = 2.650141y + 16'755'356

At pixel (100, 80) on Mario's sign:

stored depth         16'641'130
sky, own depth       0               -> 0 <= 16'641'130 passes, sky covers sign
sky, frozen plane    ~16'755'569     -> fails, sign stays visible   (y = 80.5, pixel center)
background           16'777'215      -> 16'755'569 <= 16'777'215 passes, sky fills background

Writeup: z-freeze and Mario Golf's Disappearing Menu

items.title: Flickering Floor Decals
items.text: Floor logos on the Plaza court flicker / have missing bands. Decals have nearly the same depth as the floor below them, so rounding differences make them take turns winning the depth test (Z-fighting). Sharing a depth plane via z-freeze keeps the comparison consistent.

items.title: Missing Eyes
items.text:
Mario's eyes missing on the file selection screen. The head is its own model, FileSelectDataMario, eyes use material EyeMat_v (blink animations swap its texture, see Petari).

Eye triangles are there, but every fragment fails the alpha test (blending disabled):

128 <= alpha <= 255

The open-eye texture is 64x64, every texel has alpha 255, so the texture isn't the problem.

TEV stages of the material:

  1. Stage 0 calculates an intermediate lighting value in alpha
  2. Stage 1 uses that value for color, then replaces alpha with 255
  3. Stage 2 adds a quarter of the texture alpha and a half bias, clamping disabled
alpha = 255 + 64 + 128 = 447
447 & 0xFF = 191                -> 128 <= 191 <= 255 passes

Quarter contribution: floor((255 * 64 + 128) / 256) = 64. The +128 is TEV's rounding step, not the bias (both just happen to be 128).

My old float shader did:

alpha = 1.0 + 1.0 * 0.25 + 0.5 = 1.75     -> 1.75 <= 1.0 fails

The upper bound looks redundant for an 8-bit value but isn't once a wider value reaches the comparison. Note: clamping 447 also passes (255), but that's the wrong rule. E.g. 383 wraps to 127 (fail) whereas clamping gives 255 (pass).

The decisive part of the fix is wrapping the final alpha before alpha_compare:

fn tev_wrap_alpha(value: f32) -> f32 {
    return f32(i32(round(value * 255.0)) & 255) / 255.0;
}

tev_wrap_alpha(state.regs[state.last_alpha_dest].a)

Integer arithmetic alone still leaves 447 going into the test. Adding just the helper to the old float math gives 190, the full integer calculation 191. Both pass, so the eyes coming back doesn't prove the arithmetic is right. See TEV Wrapping.

Zayd's video: The Emulator Bug that Removes Mario's Eyes

Writeup: Mario's Missing Eyes and Sunshine's White Ocean

items.title: White Ocean
items.text:
Ocean on the save selection screen is completely white. Material _mat1_1 in the menu's map.bmd draws a wave layer over the water that's already there. It reads the grayscale texture HAYAwave2 twice at different scales/offsets, intensity supplies alpha.

alpha (A, B, C, D):
stage 0: (ZERO, ZERO, ZERO, TEXA)
stage 1: (ZERO, TEXA, APREV, RASA)   scale 2x, clamp off
stage 2: (ZERO, RASA, APREV, ZERO)   clamp off          <- APREV read as C

RASA is 255. Example pixel with texture samples 93 and 121:

q     = floor((2 * 121 * 93 + 128) / 256) = 88
alpha = 2 * 255 + q = 598
C     = 598 & 0xFF = 86

The C input only keeps 8 bits. Stage 2's multiply by raster alpha preserves the 86. Alpha test accepts everything, blending is on: source factor SrcAlpha, destination SrcClr with white RGB, so it's additive brightening:

new channel = min(1, b + 86/255)

Old Gecko carried the wide value into stage 2, the constant alone was 2 * 1.0 = 2.0, saturating the water to white. Clamping would also be white, only the low byte recovers the varying wave intensity.

Note: TEV expands the C factor to C + (C >> 7) before multiplying so 255 represents exactly 1. 93 is below 128 so unchanged.

Trap: wrapping only at the final output also looks almost right (88 instead of 86) because stage 2 already did math on the wide C. Needs integer math + input wrapping. See TEV Wrapping.

Writeup: Mario's Missing Eyes and Sunshine's White Ocean

Honorary mention: neobrain, Zayd

items.title: Huge Triangles in the Sky
items.text:
Bright triangles covering the sky during the station flyby (skinned models in general). Originally debugged in Lazuli, the screenshot reproduces it in Gecko by disabling the WPAR reset.

Skinning results get written through the gather pipe into RAM (CSkinnedModel::Calculate, allocation/cache/morphing omitted):

pipe = GXRedirectWriteGatherPipe(verts);

BuildAccumulatedTransforms(pose, layout);
BuildPoints(pipe);
// Pad the position region to a multiple of 32 bytes.
BuildNormals(pipe);

GXRestoreWriteGatherPipe();
  • CVirtualBone::BuildPoints small-count path writes X, Y, Z through the same pointer without incrementing (it's the gather port)
  • GXRedirectWriteGatherPipe flushes, waits for transfers, rewrites WPAR (same 0x0C008000), disconnects the FIFOs, saves the old PI write pointer and points PI at the workspace
  • GX later reads the arrays with base address + stride

The affected pass had 23 zero bytes pending when redirecting. Without the WPAR reset they became the start of the new workspace:

reset        offset    bytes
---------------------------------------------------
yes          0         3E A0 F9 08 3E 39 E0 1A ...
no           0-22      00 ... 00 (23 zeros)
no           23        3E A0 F9 08 3E 39 E0 1A ...

All 4'224 bytes match when shifted by 23. Data was right, stored in the wrong place. GX reads with stride 12 (3 floats), array index 12:

axis    reset          no reset
-----------------------------------------
X       0.106061       0.00956970
Y       0.183704       -3.21470e15
Z       0              8.68805e-44

Broken Y is D9 36 BC 00: negative, exponent 178 -> 2^(178-127) = 2^51. Huge before projection already, same shift also breaks the normals (lighting).

Writeup: WPAR: Why Metroid Prime's Geometry Exploded

Honorary mention: vxpm

items.title: Donald's Feet Explode
items.text:
Donald's idle animation in the laboratory starts fine, then his feet stretch and his body folds into itself. Left running, triangles cover the whole room. Same with JIT and interpreter.

Positions were already wrong in RAM (CPU skinning), so GX was fine. Worked back: vertex writes -> bone matrices -> animation keyframes -> keyframe records loaded from ARAM via DMA.

Records are 24 bytes, so most aren't 32-byte aligned. The game requests 64 bytes around the record and picks it out in the completion callback, using the original unaligned address. Record at 0x7888:

  1. DMA ignores the low 5 bits, copies from 0x7880
  2. Callback: record is 8 bytes into its block
  3. Callback skips 8 bytes and copies 24

I didn't mask the DMA registers, so DMA started at 0x7888 and the callback skipped another 8:

expected:  B + r
gecko:     (B + r) + r = B + 2r

Offsets go 16, 8, 0, 24 and repeat, so 1 in 4 records still worked. At 8/16 the extracted bytes straddle 2 records, at 24 it reads the next record entirely.

From bytes to a broken bone (example with the game's rules):

  • Time 33.54, current keyframe 25, next keyframe 0 -> t = (33.54 - 25) / (0 - 25) ≈ -0.3416 (extrapolating)
  • Slerp uses a stored angle and a sine table (4'096 entries per turn). Record says 113 units (~0.17334 rad), but the quaternions are actually arccos(0.70769) ≈ 0.78457 rad apart
  • k = trunc(0.5 + t*N) = -38, weights a = sin(151π/2048) / sin(113π/2048) ≈ 1.33102, b = sin(-38π/2048) / sin(113π/2048) ≈ -0.33778
  • |q|² = a² + b² + 2ab(q0·q1) -> |q| ≈ 1.118 instead of 1
  • Quaternion-to-matrix doesn't normalize -> bone stretches, propagates to children -> skinning

Every calculation did what it was supposed to, the bytes were just wrong.

Writeup: Goin' Quackers: Why Donald's Feet Exploded

items.title: Memory
items.text: write-gather pipe and DMA notes, mostly things that corrupt data before GX ever sees it. See Games for the bugs these caused

items.title: WPAR Reset
items.text:
Gekko's write-gather pipe combines stores into 32-byte bursts. Games write to 0xCC008000 (physical 0x0C008000, selected by WPAR) and PI writes each burst to RAM at its FIFO write pointer. Software can point PI somewhere else and disconnect GX's FIFO to build arrays in RAM.

A mtspr to WPAR invalidates the data in the buffer and sets the gather address. Source

Writing WPAR (SPR 921) discards pending bytes even if the address doesn't change. Bytes already transferred stay in RAM. Without the reset, leftover bytes end up at the start of the next buffer and shift everything.

GXRestoreWriteGatherPipe writes 31 zero bytes before restoring the FIFO: a partial burst has 1-31 useful bytes, so 31 zeros guarantee the useful tail leaves in a complete burst. The leftover padding is then discarded by the WPAR write. Order matters (pad, then reset)!

Fix (commit), needed in both interpreter and JIT runtime function:

921 => {
    sys.gekko.spr.wpar = val & !1; // bit 0 is BNE (read-only buffer status)
    sys.cp.gather_pos = 0;         // empty the pipe, no need to zero the buffer
}

Same commit also fixed redirection: PI must keep writing bursts to RAM while the CPU/GPU FIFOs are disconnected. Only the GX notification depends on the link:

write the complete burst to RAM
advance the PI write pointer

if the GPU FIFO is linked:
    update its write pointer and available byte count

retain only the incomplete tail for the next burst

items.title: ARAM DMA
items.text:
ARAM DMA works in 32-byte blocks. Main RAM address, ARAM address and length are all masked with 0x03FF_FFE0 (bit 31 of length is direction). Same masks as Dolphin.

Games may write unaligned addresses on purpose and rely on the hardware ignoring the low bits.

Fix (commit):

const ARAM_DMA_MASK: u32 = 0x03ff_ffe0;

address = written_address & ARAM_DMA_MASK;
control = written_control & (0x8000_0000 | ARAM_DMA_MASK);
  • Apply on every register write
  • Apply on savestate load too (older states may contain unmasked values)
  • Writing the lower half of the length register starts the transfer, upper half alone doesn't

items.title: OTP
items.text:
OTP (one-time programmable memory) stores 128 bytes inside Hollywood. It is programmed during manufacturing and cannot be erased or rewritten. Its contents include the expected boot1 hash and cryptographic keys (TODO: anything else?).

The first 20 bytes hold the expected boot1 hash, see boot0 reads this field during verification.

items.title: Boot sequence
items.text:
1. boot0 decrypts and verifies boot1
  2. boot1 loads, decrypts and verifies boot2
  3. boot2 hands off into IOS
  4. IOS does whatever bullshit for System Menu, probably also EXI stuff

items.title: boot0
items.text: Boot0 reads boot1 from NAND into SRAM, corrects read errors, decrypts it and checks its hash against OTP before handing over execution. See the Starlet memory map for SRAM and ROM mappings.

items.title: Entry and buffers
items.text: ARM address Use 0xFFFF0000 Reset vector 0xFFFF0040 reset: sets the stack pointer and enters the loader 0xFFFF0108 load_boot1 0x0D400000-0x0D4177FF boot1 buffer, 94 KiB 0x0D417800 First spare/ECC buffer 0x0D417880 Second spare/ECC buffer 0x0D417C00 Initial stack pointer 0xFFF00000 boot1 entry through the SRAM alias

items.title: Loading and verification
items.text:
load_boot1 writes 7 to HW_SRNPROT, enabling SRAM access for NAND, SHA-1 and AES while leaving SM clear. It loads the AES key and IV from ROM and reads five OTP words, starting at index 0, as the expected hash.

expected_hash = OTP_ReadWords(0, 5);

for (page = 0; page < 47; page++) {
    NAND_ReadPage(page, boot1 + page * 2048, spare);
    if (!ECC_CorrectPage(boot1 + page * 2048, spare))
        fatal_error(0xF1);
}

AES_CBC_Decrypt(boot1, 0x17800, rom_key, rom_iv);
actual_hash = SHA1_CalculateBlocks(boot1, 0x17800);

if (!AllZero(expected_hash) && actual_hash != expected_hash)
    fatal_error(0xF2);

jump(0xFFF00000);

items.text:
Code Meaning 0xF1 Uncorrectable ECC error 0xF2 boot1 hash mismatch

fatal_error repeatedly writes the code to GPIO bits 23:16, delays, writes zero, and delays again.

items.title: NAND
items.text: All of this is written assuming a HY27UF084G2M NAND chip.

items.title: Makeup
items.text:
The NAND is made up of a list of clusters. Each cluster is made of 64 pages, and each page is made up of 2K (0x800) bytes, plus an additional spare 64 bytes. The spare can be used for various purposes, for example being able to tell if a block is bad, or detecting corruption using ECC. The first byte of the spare is 0xFF iff the block is valid. The last 16 bytes of spare seem to contain the software-calculated ECC for the page.

[!WARNING] On startup, boot2 will do an initial scan of all blocks. For any blocks it detects are bad (by reading the first byte of spare), it will clear out the cluster.

items.title: Reads
items.text:
The NAND seems to have an internal buffer of size 0x840 - the exact length of a page plus its spare. Reads seem to follow two phases. First, read the data from the actual NAND storage into the internal buffer. Then, read the buffer out of the device, into the Starlet.

The Starlet will usually initiate three commands in quick succession when it wants to perform a read:

  1. 0x00 (Seems to move the requested page into the internal buffer)
  2. 0x01 (ditto, but for the spare bytes?)
  3. 0x30 (Read confirm - actually do the read)

This is all well and good. It would be, if the NAND interface wasn't written by a fucking dumbass. There's two buffers provided by the Starlet to the NAND interface - NAND_DATABUF and NAND_ECCBUF.

Well, actually THREE buffers, because there's a hidden third buffer at NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40. The three buffers operate in ways that defy logic:

  1. The first 0x800 bytes that are read, whatever they may be, goes in NAND_DATABUF.
  2. The next 0x40 bytes, if they are read, must be the spare. And so they go in NAND_ECCBUF. Notably, there is an issue in nomenclature and this should probably be called NAND_SPAREBUF but I digress.
  3. And finally, 0x10 bytes of hardware-calculated ECC are written to NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40.

[!TIP] If you happen to be writing an emulator... just write the last 0x10 bytes of the spare out to NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40. Saves you from having to do an ECC calculation yourself :) I honestly just discovered that I can create these cool Tip / Warning blocks and am getting a kick out of it.

items.title: Cluster Erases
items.text:
There are two commands sent to erase stuff:

  1. 0x60 (program in the cluster you want to erase)
  2. 0xD0 (confirm, do the erase)

Boot2's NAND_EraseCluster function looks roughly like this: 

int NAND_EraseCluster(uint cluster) {
  int result;
  astruct_2 *iVar1;

  if (cluster < (uint)(1 << (_MAX_CLUSTERS - 14 & 0xff))) {
    // possibly NAND_Initialized?
    if (_DAT_20009000 == 0) {
      nand_status = -10;
    } else {
      _NAND_CONFIG = _NAND_CONFIG & 0x7fffffff;

      Nand_ProgramRowCol(-1, cluster << (0xeU - _DAT_2004f1a4 & 0xff));

      result = Nand_SendCommand(0x60, a1_through_5_requested_set_erase & 0x1c,0,0);
      if (result != 0) {
        // enable interrupts
        result = Nand_SendCommand(0xD0,0,0x40008000,0);
        if (result != 0) {
            result = Nand_ReadStatus();
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    result = -4;
  }

  _NAND_CONFIG = _NAND_CONFIG | 0x80000000;

  // who knows, and honestly who cares
  FUN_13a10048(cluster,0,nand_status);

  return result;
}

items.title: Getting to Shell
items.text:
In my testing a few things are required to be able to progress to the BIOS shell:

  • Being at the diamond screen (duh...)
  • Timer or at least forcing 0xFF on reads
  • VBLANK IRQ (kind of... without it I get stuck in a blue screen)
  • CDROM with a few basic commands and IRQ

Note: unmapped reads return 0xFF for me!! Depending on that value results may differ.

items.title: CDROM Commands
items.text:
The following commands seem to be required as a bare minimum:

cmd     subcmd  irq     result fifo
----------------------------------------------
0x01            INT3    Status
0x19    0x20    INT3    Get cdrom BIOS date/version (yy,mm,dd,ver)

items.title: Further Notes & Code
items.text:
• I return [0x69, 0x69, 0x69, 0x69] for the CDROM version
  • I set only the "Shell Open" bit for status
  • I send both "acknowledge" and "complete" IRQs (with an arbitrary 1000 cycle delay inbetween)
  • I update parameter readiness bits on every tick
fn execute_command(&mut self, command: u8) {
    match command {
        // 0x01     Nop         INT3: status
        0x01 => {
            self.pending_command = Some(command);
            self.send_status(&[]);
            self.trigger_irq(DiskIrq::CommandAcknowledged);
        }
        // 0x19     Test *  sub, ...    INT3: ...
        0x19 => {
            let subcommand = self.parameter_fifo.pop_front().unwrap();
            self.execute_subcommand(subcommand);
        }
        _ => {
            tracing::error!(
                target: "psx_core::cdrom",
                command = format!("{:02X}", command),
                "Unimplemented CDROM command",
            );
        }
    }

    self.address.set_busy_status(true);
}

fn execute_subcommand(&mut self, subcommand: u8) {
    match subcommand {
        0x20 => {
            self.result_fifo.push_back(0x69); // year
            self.result_fifo.push_back(0x69); // month
            self.result_fifo.push_back(0x69); // day
            self.result_fifo.push_back(0x69); // version
            self.trigger_irq(DiskIrq::CommandAcknowledged);
        }
    }
}

pub fn tick(&mut self, cycles: usize) {
    self.address.set_parameter_empty(self.parameter_fifo.is_empty());
    self.address.set_parameter_write_ready(self.parameter_fifo.len() < 16);
    self.cycles += cycles;

    if self.cycles >= CYCLE_DELAY {
        self.cycles -= CYCLE_DELAY;

        if let Some(command) = self.pending_command.take() {
            self.parameter_fifo.clear();
            self.address.set_busy_status(false);
            self.address.set_data_request(true);
            self.address.set_result_read_ready(true);

            self.trigger_irq(DiskIrq::CommandCompleted);
        }
    }
}

items.title: BIOS Stuck in Loop
items.text:
Stubbed GPUSTAT (0xFFFF_FFFF) will eventually lead to this:

loc_8004FE44:
lw      $a4, 0($a1)
addiu   $v1, $v1, 1
xor     $a5, $v0, $a4
and     $a6, $a5, $a0
beq     $a6, $zero, loc_8004FE44
nop

where:

  • a0 is 0x8000_0000
  • a1 points to GPUSTAT register
  • v0 is original GPUSTAT value

Basically waits for bit 31 to change.

In 480-lines mode, bit31 changes per frame. And in 240-lines mode, the bit changes per scanline. The bit is always zero during Vblank (vertical retrace and upper/lower screen border).

Seems to be 240-lines mode in my case. We get here because of the start of that routine:

sub_8004FE08:
lw      $v0, 0($a1)
bne     $a0, $zero, loc_8004FF00
lui     $at, 8
and     $t6, $v0, $at
beq     $t6, $zero, loc_8004FE64
nop

Roughly translates to (same register meaning as above): 

if ( (*GPUSTAT & 0x80000) != 0 ) {
  // Deadlock here...
}

It checks bit 19, if it's not 0 it will start waiting for something. This bit indicates vertical resolution:

  • 0 = 240 lines (what it should be according to my emulator atm)
  • 1 = 480 lines

So if the vertical resolution is 480 lines it will start waiting for a new frame presumably? Since the next bit change (bit 31) would be during VBLANK (???). Since GPUSTAT is stubbed it will always think we are in 480 lines mode. 0x1480_2000 seems to work better as an early stub (reset value?) but breaks the amidog CPU tests unless bit 27 which indicates VRAM to CPU DMA readiness is forcefully set as well.

Note: BIOS does swap to 480-lines mode eventually, so can't really escape it for long.

items.title: Calculating Polygon Word Count
items.text:
Polygon primitive base count is calculated based on vertices count bit:

pub struct DrawPolygonCommand(pub u32) {
    pub color: u32 @ 0..=23,
    pub raw_texture: bool @ 24,
    pub semi_transparent: bool @ 25,
    pub textured: bool @ 26,
    pub vertices_count: bool @ 27,
    pub gouraud: bool @ 28,
    pub command: u32 @ 29..=31,
}

Base count of extra data words is either 4 or 3 (will call the count vertices). 4 if vertices_count is set.

  • If gouraud is set, then vertices - 1 on top of that
  • If textured is set, then vertices

Basically: 

Gp0Command::PolygonPrimitive(cmd) => {
    let vertices = if cmd.vertices_count() { 4 } else { 3 };
    let mut base = vertices;

    // requires color for vertices 1..n (color 0 in cmd word)
    if cmd.gouraud() {
        base += vertices - 1;
    }

    // requires UV for each vertex (no vertex in cmd word)
    if cmd.textured() {
        base += vertices;
    }

    base
}

items.title: Rasterizer
items.text:
Given vertices v0, v1, v2, v3 to draw a rectangle/quad: 

v0 --- v1        Triangle 1: v0 -> v1 -> v2
|       |        Triangle 2: v1 -> v2 -> v3
|       |
v2 --- v3        Note: 0-indexed, see below

Quads are internally processed as two triangles, the first consisting of vertices 1,2,3, and the second of vertices 2,3,4. Source

fn rasterize_polygon(vertices: &[(i16, i16)], colors: &[u32], vram: &mut [u8]) {
    // fun stuff
}
  • If vertices.len() == 4 then we know we have a quad and must split it into 2 triangles
  • If not, then we operate on "Triangle 1" only
  • colors maps each coordinate with a color which can later be used for coloring and applying gradient
  • vram is just a reference to the internal VRAM storage

To get the coordinate/corner positions: 

let (x0, y0) = (vertices[0].0 as i32, vertices[0].1 as i32);
let (x1, y1) = (vertices[1].0 as i32, vertices[1].1 as i32);
let (x2, y2) = (vertices[2].0 as i32, vertices[2].1 as i32);

For optimization we can define a min/max (bounding box?) of the polygon so we can perform the math on this selection only: 

let min_x = x0.min(x1).min(x2).max(0);
let max_x = x0.max(x1).max(x2).min(VRAM_WIDTH as i32 - 1);
let min_y = y0.min(y1).min(y2).max(0);
let max_y = y0.max(y1).max(y2).min(VRAM_HEIGHT as i32 - 1);

  • min_x: The leftmost point of any corner
  • max_x: The rightmost point of any corner
  • min_y: The topmost point of any corner
  • max_y: The bottommost point of any corner

Now to fill a triangle we'll have to go through each point in the bounding box (?) and check whether this point is:

  • to the left of a line A to B
  • to the right of a line A to B
  • on top of a line A to B
fn edge_function(ax: i32, ay: i32, bx: i32, by: i32, px: i32, py: i32) -> i32 {
    (bx - ax) * (py - ay) - (by - ay) * (px - ax)
}

let area = edge_function(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2); // if area == 0 -> straight line
let clockwise = area < 0;

let w0 = edge_function(x1, y1, x2, y2, x, y);
let w1 = edge_function(x2, y2, x0, y0, x, y);
let w2 = edge_function(x0, y0, x1, y1, x, y);

let inside = if clockwise {
    w0 <= 0 && w1 <= 0 && w2 <= 0
} else {
    w0 >= 0 && w1 >= 0 && w2 >= 0
};

// if inside == true -> pixel x,y is inside of triangle

To interpolate the colors: 

let r0 = (colors[0] & 0xFF) as i32;
let g0 = ((colors[0] >> 8) & 0xFF) as i32;
let b0 = ((colors[0] >> 16) & 0xFF) as i32;

let r1 = (colors[1] & 0xFF) as i32;
let g1 = ((colors[1] >> 8) & 0xFF) as i32;
let b1 = ((colors[1] >> 16) & 0xFF) as i32;

let r2 = (colors[2] & 0xFF) as i32;
let g2 = ((colors[2] >> 8) & 0xFF) as i32;
let b2 = ((colors[2] >> 16) & 0xFF) as i32;

// gouraud shading
let r = (r0 * w0 + r1 * w1 + r2 * w2) / area;
let g = (g0 * w0 + g1 * w1 + g2 * w2) / area;
let b = (b0 * w0 + b1 * w1 + b2 * w2) / area;

Since VRAM stores RGB values as RGB555 we'll have to modify them: 

let r5 = ((r >> 3) & 0x1F) as u16;
let g5 = ((g >> 3) & 0x1F) as u16;
let b5 = ((b >> 3) & 0x1F) as u16;
let pixel = (b5 << 10) | (g5 << 5) | r5;

items.title: Controller Input Issues
items.text:
Directional controls (up/down) on this screen might not work (even though other buttons work). This happens if SIO0 RX is sent for both ports at the same time (bit 13).

0     TX Enable (TXEN)      (0=Disable, 1=Enable)
1     DTR Output Level      (0=Off, 1=On)
2     RX Enable (RXEN)      (SIO1: 0=Disable, 1=Enable)  ;Disable also clears RXFIFO
                            (SIO0: 0=only receive when /CS low, 1=force receiving single byte)
3     SIO1 TX Output Level  (0=Normal, 1=Inverted, during Inactivity & Stop bits)
4     Acknowledge           (0=No change, 1=Reset SIO_STAT.Bits 3,4,5,9)      (W)
5     SIO1 RTS Output Level (0=Off, 1=On)
6     Reset                 (0=No change, 1=Reset most registers to zero) (W)
7     SIO1 unknown?         (read/write-able when FACTOR non-zero) (otherwise always zero)
8-9   RX Interrupt Mode     (0..3 = IRQ when RX FIFO contains 1,2,4,8 bytes)
10    TX Interrupt Enable   (0=Disable, 1=Enable) ;when SIO_STAT.0-or-2 ;Ready
11    RX Interrupt Enable   (0=Disable, 1=Enable) ;when N bytes in RX FIFO
12    DSR Interrupt Enable  (0=Disable, 1=Enable) ;when SIO_STAT.7  ;DSR high or /ACK low
13    SIO0 port select      (0=port 1, 1=port 2) (/CS pulled low when bit 1 set)
14-15 Not used              (always zero)

Based on bit 13 only respond for the selected port. In my case I ignore port 2 (returning 0xFF denotes absence).

match tx_byte {
    0x01 => {
        if self.control.port_number() == 2 {
            // If Port 2 is selected, no controller is present
            tracing::trace!(
                target: "psx_core::sio",
                tx = format!("{:02X}", tx_byte),
                "Port 2 selected - no device"
            );
            return 0xFF;
        }

        self.active_device = ActiveDevice::Controller;
    }
    0x81 => {
        self.active_device = ActiveDevice::MemoryCard;
    }
    _ => {}
}

When SIO0_CTRL is written, I also check whether the port number changed to 2 and reset the state machine if necessary: 

if matches!(self.active_device, ActiveDevice::None | ActiveDevice::Controller)
    && self.control.port_number() == 2
{
    self.reset_devices();
}

Honorary mention: Chicho

items.title: Fragmented Graphics
items.text:
Polygon commands must propagate their texpage to the global texpage.

// Update global texpage state from polygon's embedded texpage
// Texpage is in uvs[1] upper 16 bits (same location as for triangles/quads)
if uvs.len() > 1 {
    let texpage = ((uvs[1] >> 16) & 0xFFFF) as u16;

    // Extract texpage components (bits 0-8, 11 update global state)
    let texture_page_x_base = (texpage & 0xF) as u32;
    let texture_page_y_base_1 = ((texpage >> 4) & 0x1) != 0;
    let texture_page_colors = ((texpage >> 7) & 0x3) as u32;
    let texture_page_y_base_2 = ((texpage >> 11) & 0x1) != 0;

    // Update global GPU state (same as GP0(E1h) command)
    self.gp.gp1_status.set_texture_page_x_base(texture_page_x_base);
    self.gp.gp1_status.set_texture_page_y_base_1(texture_page_y_base_1);
    self.gp.gp1_status.set_texture_page_colors(texture_page_colors);
    self.gp.gp1_status.set_texture_page_y_base_2(texture_page_y_base_2);
}

Honorary mention: Lycoder

items.title: Missing Graphics
items.text:
Missing VRAM to VRAM Blit command, something along the lines of:

let src_x = (parsed_cmd.data[0] & 0xFFFF) as u16;
let src_y = ((parsed_cmd.data[0] >> 16) & 0xFFFF) as u16;
let dst_x = (parsed_cmd.data[1] & 0xFFFF) as u16;
let dst_y = ((parsed_cmd.data[1] >> 16) & 0xFFFF) as u16;
let width = (parsed_cmd.data[2] & 0xFFFF) as usize;
let height = ((parsed_cmd.data[2] >> 16) & 0xFFFF) as usize;

// Copy rectangle from source to destination in VRAM
// Handle overlapping regions by copying to a temporary buffer first
let mut temp_buffer: Vec<u16> = Vec::with_capacity(width * height);

// Read from source
for row in 0..height {
    for col in 0..width {
        let vram_x = (src_x as usize + col) & (VRAM_WIDTH - 1);
        let vram_y = (src_y as usize + row) & (VRAM_HEIGHT - 1);
        let vram_idx = (vram_y * VRAM_WIDTH + vram_x) * 2;
        let byte0 = self.gp.vram[vram_idx];
        let byte1 = self.gp.vram[vram_idx + 1];
        let pixel = u16::from_le_bytes([byte0, byte1]);
        temp_buffer.push(pixel);
    }
}

// Write to destination
let mut pixel_idx = 0;
for row in 0..height {
    for col in 0..width {
        let vram_x = (dst_x as usize + col) & (VRAM_WIDTH - 1);
        let vram_y = (dst_y as usize + row) & (VRAM_HEIGHT - 1);
        let vram_idx = (vram_y * VRAM_WIDTH + vram_x) * 2;
        let bytes = temp_buffer[pixel_idx].to_le_bytes();
        self.gp.vram[vram_idx] = bytes[0];
        self.gp.vram[vram_idx + 1] = bytes[1];
        pixel_idx += 1;
    }
}
